Vidya has answered "fine" to every question about how she is for three weeks. When I asked after class today, she said, "Nothing, ma'am. Just a headache." She has mentioned headaches four times this month, and a stiff neck. She sits at the edge of the group at lunch.

What I did next: I asked the counsellor to meet her gently, and I'll call her parents today about the headaches, so they can check with the doctor if they keep going.

In the college hostel's common room, Mahima sat with Aditi, her roommate of two years, and finally said it.
"You never tell me anything. When my grandmother was sick, I told you everything. When your parents split, you just said 'it's fine'. I feel like I don't matter to you."

Elizabeth, you said your fiancé never tells you what he feels. Let me tell you a story about a man who couldn't.
I was twenty-five, newly married. My wife would ask, "What's wrong?" and I'd say "Nothing." And I believed it. I only knew my chest was tight or my jaw hurt. I thought I was just tired.
One day she cried and said, "It's like living with a wall." That scared me.
So I started, awkwardly. I wrote feeling words on a sheet and stuck it inside my cupboard. Every night I wrote two lines: what my body felt, what word might fit. "Chest tight. Nervous? Angry?" When it still felt like shouting in a dark room, I went to a counsellor, which in those days took some courage.
I'm Lalit, and it took two years. But my wife says I talk too much now.
